title: Wrexham pushed Chelsea to the limit. Are they ready for the Premier League?
content:
There was quite a crowd building outside the Wrexham Lager Stand on Saturday afternoon: children, parents, grandparents, all waiting for a glimpse of their heroes and perhaps, if they were lucky, an autograph or a selfie.

Wrexham’s players were happy to oblige. Kick-off was barely an hour away, an FA Cup fifth-round glamour tie against Chelsea that would leave a huge global TV audience enthralled, but one player after another did the rounds, signing every shirt, match programme, ball or scrap of paper that was eagerly thrust in front of them.

“Big game, is it?” defender Max Cleworth joked with the fans, remarking on the size of the crowd. He was a teenager, trying to establish himself in the fifth-tier National League, when Wrexham were bought by Hollywood stars Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac in early 2021. The club’s fortunes have been transformed over the five years since, but even with A-list celebrities in the stands, lending an air of celebrity that seems at odds with this unpretentious North Wales town, a sense of earthiness endures.

When the Wrexham players had finally done their pre-match walkabout, the stewards told the supporters to move back because the Chelsea team were on their way. Barriers were moved back to allow the bus to get as close to the players’ entrance as possible. One by one, they walked stony-faced past the crowd — Reece James, Marc Cucurella, Joao Pedro, Pedro Neto, Alejandro Garnacho, some with headphones on, others with hoods up — and straight through the door to the sanctuary of the dressing room.

Some of the parents, who had been hoping Chelsea’s players would stop for photos with the little ones, were disappointed. But the kids didn’t seem concerned. One boy said the only Chelsea players he was interested in were Cole Palmer and Enzo Fernandez and they had not been on the bus. That same boy had just spent half an hour gawping at Wrexham’s players: towering goalkeeper Arthur Okonkwo, defender Callum Doyle, new signing Zak Vyner, midfielders George Dobson and Ollie Rathbone and striker Sam Smith.

Other clubs’ fans might be indifferent or indeed hostile to Wrexham’s Hollywood-backed story, which is too sickly-sweet for many tastes, but something important is happening. In an age when kids are so easily drawn to the biggest players and teams, the ones they see on TV and the Xbox, it is refreshing to walk through the town centre and see so many Wrexham shirts rather than the more familiar red of Liverpool or Manchester United, both less than 50 miles away.

The way Saturday’s FA Cup tie unfolded is only likely to help Wrexham’s bid to win hearts and minds locally, never mind across the Atlantic. They were beaten 4-2 by Chelsea, but only after leading twice and looking the more likely winners until they had Dobson sent off in stoppage time at the end of 90 minutes. Chelsea proved too strong in extra time, with an extra man. But even then, Lewis Brunt thought he had scored a dramatic equaliser for Wrexham, only for the delirious celebrations to be followed by a VAR check which found he had been offside when he turned in Kieffer Moore’s flick-on.

Wrexham were terrific — “magnificent in their energy, how brave they were in the press and how they played”, as Chelsea coach Liam Rosenior put it. They fed from the energy of a passionate crowd at the Stok Cae Ras, but that has become a two-way relationship. “The team has got to reflect the town,” their manager Phil Parkinson said afterwards. “That is what the people of Wrexham want. That is what we’ve always tried to do.”

There are few things more uplifting in team sports than the sight of a town and a group of players driving each other on, hardly daring to dream just how far a journey might take them.

This, remarkably, is where Wrexham find themselves in 2026, not just beating Nottingham Forest in the FA Cup third round and taking Chelsea the distance in round five, but knocking on the door of the Premier League, sixth in the Championship and on course for the end-of-season promotion play-offs. If this FA Cup run has given the supporters a taste of the really big time, they have enjoyed it.

This is a club that spent 15 years in the wilderness of non-League football, wondering if they would ever get back. My previous visit had been in 2017 for an interview with their beloved former player Mickey Thomas, scorer of an FA Cup wonder goal in a famous victory over the mighty Arsenal in 1992.

Wrexham were in a stage of stagnation at the time and the Racecourse Ground, as it was known in those days, in a state of disrepair. Thomas remarked that it was sad to see the club in such hard times, but he pointed out it had been much worse in the turbulent years before that when its existence came under severe threat.

In many ways, the place hasn’t changed. The biggest difference is that the old Kop terrace, which stood derelict for years, has finally been demolished, with a new stand now under construction. What has truly changed is the energy around the club. It feels like it has been electrified.

British football in the 21st century has been an ownership lottery. So many clubs have fallen victim to unsuitable ownership and abject mismanagement, dragged down far beyond their natural level. A small number of others have struck lucky and found benefactors willing — motivations vary — and able to build on whatever foundations have been in place.

Chelsea’s history was transformed when they were bought by the Russian billionaire Roman Abramovich in 2003. Wrexham’s history has been transformed, at least in the short term, by Reynolds’ and Mac’s crazy idea to buy a non-League club in North Wales and have a bit of fun with it.

Hollywood stars Will Ferrell, Hugh Jackman, Eva Longoria and Channing Tatum have shown up to watch Wrexham at various points over the last few years. On Saturday evening the co-owners were joined by Reynolds’ actress wife Blake Lively.

And if you were watching on television, you might well have found yourself wearied by just how often the cameras cut to the VIP seats so we could see just what Reynolds and Mac were making of it all. At some point further down the line, when the next season of the Welcome to Wrexham documentary is released, we might get a clearer insight.

But those of us lucky enough to be inside the Stok Cae Ras could hear and see and feel what Wrexham’s fans made of it. It was loud, passionate and raw, belting out Men of Harlech and Land of my Fathers, and the celebrations that greeted Smith’s opening goal in the 18th minute and Doyle’s strike in the 78th minute (to restore Wrexham’s lead, albeit briefly) were ferocious in their intensity.

Ah, VAR. There’s something Wrexham didn’t have to worry about in the National League. Nor in the Championship in fact. Or even in the previous rounds of the FA Cup. So if this tie had taken place in the third or fourth round, Dobson would have got away with his wild challenge on Garnacho, while Brunt would have got away with knocking the ball in from an offside position. “F*** VAR, f*** VAR,” echoed all around the ground — a sentiment most of us have shared in recent years, even if, in this instance, there could be no serious argument over either decision.

“I thought we were in the game all the way to the red card,” Wrexham midfielder Vyner said afterwards. “That was our first taste of VAR and… it is what it is. Tonight I don’t want it, but it’s part of the game. There’s no getting away from it now. And hopefully it’s not the last time we have it because we’re striving to play with VAR every week.”

What Vyner meant is that Wrexham want to be in the Premier League, where VAR interventions are recognised as part of the landscape. With 11 games left to play in the regular Championship season, starting at home to Hull City on Tuesday evening, qualification for the promotion play-offs looks well within their capabilities.

But even after a day like Saturday, the Premier League must sometimes feel like another world for Parkinson and his players. Yes they pushed Chelsea hard, but it was a Chelsea squad without Palmer, Fernandez and Moises Caicedo, with James an unused substitute, while Cucurella, Joao Pedro and Malo Gusto were only summoned from the bench in the second half. And still the starting line-up contained young players such as Jorrel Hato, Andrey Santos and Garnacho, who are full internationals for the Netherlands, Brazil and Argentina respectively.

“It’s a huge gulf in spending power between the Premier League and where we are in the Championship and where we’ve come so quickly,” Parkinson said afterwards.

It is hard to see that changing. For all the emphasis on Wrexham’s spending under their American owners, the financial advantages they enjoyed at National League, League Two and League One level are not felt anything like so clearly in the Championship and would not be in the Premier League, where they would be competing — not just in one-off games like this, but every week — against clubs who, in terms of infrastructure and financial strength, are at a level far beyond.

Right now, Wrexham are in a sweet spot, still on an upward trajectory, still surpassing their supporters’ wildest dreams and still — despite their unlikely appeal to the American market — a team so intimately connected to their town and the fans on their doorstep. There was no Hollywood ending on Saturday. The occasion felt too authentic for that.
